claims.text: The as-synthesized nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs solid solution is highly disordered at the atomic scale.
Mild low-temperature annealing will induce slight local atomic ordering in the catalyst.
Mild low-temperature annealing will modify the catalyst's surface strain.
The annealing treatment can change local ordering and strain without changing overall elemental composition.
Local atomic ordering and surface strain govern adsorption energies of ethanol-oxidation intermediates on PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Acetaldehyde and acetate are key intermediates whose adsorption energies are relevant to the proposed selectivity change.
Changing intermediate adsorption energies will shift ethanol-oxidation pathway selectivity.
Heterogeneous neighboring sites with different local electronic structures in high-entropy alloys can tune selectivity in complex reactions.
IrOsPtPdRhRu can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
A 12-electron ethanol-oxidation pathway represents complete oxidation rather than partial oxidation.
Annealing may favor complete 12-electron oxidation over partial oxidation.
The annealed catalyst will show a measurable change in the adsorption energies and distribution of reaction intermediates relative to the pristine catalyst.
The annealed catalyst will show a different product-selectivity profile under otherwise identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
In situ or ex situ spectroscopy and microscopy can establish the proposed annealing-induced changes in local ordering and strain.
The hypothesis applies under standard ethanol-oxidation temperatures, electrolytes, and electrochemical potentials, provided annealing does not alter overall composition.
Minor treatment variations and uncontrolled nanoscale factors may affect the magnitude of adsorption-energy and selectivity changes.
A statistically significant comparison against an identically tested as-synthesized control can test the predicted adsorption and selectivity changes.
Failure to observe a statistically significant adsorption-energy or product-selectivity difference would falsify the hypothesis.
